findings.problem: The direction's whole promise is that editing is pulling something nearer on a measure that means time. Driving it, nothing moves: I pressed the week-earlier stepper twelve times at 1440 and the row teleports to each new top, because .b-item carries no transition on top and move() writes item.style.top synchronously. The only motion anywhere in the master is border-colour and background-colour at 0.14s on .b-switch, .b-act and .b-grab. So the one moment this design exists to make felt is a jump cut, and across all eleven states there is no memorable moment at all. It reads as a very well-drawn poster, not a thing that answers you back.
findings.fix: In b.css add to .b-item: transition: top 0.22s cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1); (the global prefers-reduced-motion block at shell.css line 202 already neutralises it). In render-b.js move(), write the new top inside a requestAnimationFrame so the transition actually runs, and count the .b-away figure from its old value to its new one across the same 0.22s instead of swapping the string, so the number and the position travel together. Add an assertion to interaction-check.mjs that .b-item has a non-zero transition-duration for top, and that the item's top is still between its start and end value 80ms after a stepper press.

findings.element: .b-date, the .b-grab aria-label, .b-gapNote and .b-stepRead after a stepper press
findings.problem: move() updates only data-away, style.top, .b-away and the readout. After one press the row shows the count 1 beside its own date label SAT 8 AUG; the horizon still says 'Nothing is planned for the next 16 days' while something is now one day away; the row's accessible name still says 'in 23 days'; and the readout changes from 'Saturday 8 August 2026 · in 23 days' to 'in 1 days' — dropping the date, which is the only fact a planner is moving, and printing '1 days'. Twelve presses also drive the moved row through its neighbour (one collision). A planner who moves the invitations and watches the date refuse to follow will not hand this to a couple. The measured gate passes every part of it because it only checks the count.
findings.fix: In render-b.js move(), derive the new date once — var next = F.addDays(F.today(), current) — and write every dependent fact from that single value: item.querySelector('.b-date').textContent = F.fmt.weekdayShort(next) + ' ' + F.fmt.short(next); rebuild the .b-grab aria-label with the same string builder used at first paint; read.textContent = F.fmt.longYear(next) + ' · in ' + current + (current === 1 ? ' day' : ' days'); and re-run the horizon's gap-note accessor so .b-gapNote is recomputed from the live item set. Re-run the collision guard after every move, not only at first paint. Add to interaction-check.mjs: after three presses of the week-earlier stepper, assert .b-date, the aria-label, .b-stepRead and .b-gapNote all agree with the item's own date, that no visible string reads '1 days', and that no two items collide.

findings.problem: The reversibility surface is a hard-coded sentence with a dead button. It says 'Last change: the invitations moved seven days closer' before you have touched anything, it still says exactly that after twelve moves, and clicking Undo or pressing Ctrl+Z changes nothing — the edited item's top is 224 before and 224 after both. The behaviour gate passes it on all five of its assertions (it exists, there is one of it, it is a live region, it offers a control and names a key, it says what it would undo) and every one of those is satisfied by a stage prop. A surface that asserts a change which never happened, and refuses the one that did, is worse than having no undo at all.
findings.fix: Hold a stack of {id, fromAway} pushed by move(). Render .b-undo only when the stack is non-empty; generate its sentence from the top of the stack ('Last change: <title> moved <n> days closer|further'); wire both the button and a document-level Ctrl+Z / Cmd+Z handler to pop the stack, call move() with the inverse delta and return focus to the .b-step that made the change. Add to interaction-check.mjs: no .b-undo exists before any move; after a move its sentence names the item that actually moved; the button and Ctrl+Z each restore the item's top, its date, its count and its accessible name to their pre-move values.

findings.problem: This is the emotional peak of the entire product — the couple, both families and the venue open it on the morning, on a phone, and judge the company by it — and it is the emptiest screen in the set. Its complete text is 'Today / Mara & Finn / Saturday 3 October 2026 / Everything on the plan has happened. Nothing is left to count.' That is a receipt for a counter that has run out. Nobody standing in a room at 9am wants to be told nothing is left to count; they want to know the cars come at 12.40 and the ceremony is at 2. The screen with the most feeling available to it currently carries the least, and it is the screen the printed keepsake is meant to echo.
findings.fix: Give the day the day. Reuse the measure with hours in place of days: swap --px-per-day for --px-per-hour across the running order of 3 October, keep the same tick, count column and rail, make the current hour the filled tick, and replace the horizon count with the time of the next thing and what it is ('Next · 12.40 · Cars to the church'), the .b-num carrying hours rather than a zero. Keep the present closing line for after the last item has passed, worded for the evening rather than for an empty ledger. Shoot the state at all four widths and assert in interaction-check.mjs that the day surface names at least one time of day and that its tick positions are strictly proportional to hours.

findings.problem: The comment above the rule promises 'an opaque ground so nothing reads through', and then the second background declaration overrides var(--back) with var(--fore-06), computing to rgba(255,255,255,0.06). Three other item titles — Final dress fitting, Choose the evening music, Final guest numbers — read straight through the panel at 1440 and 1280, crossing the faces of the stepper buttons; at 390 it is four, and the panel is squeezed to 154px wide by 537px tall inside its absolutely-positioned item, stacking every control one word per line with 'Send the inv' clipped in the field. The owner's only real workspace is the least finished object in the master.
findings.fix: Delete the second background: var(--fore-06); on .b-edit so the background: var(--back); above it stands, and add box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgba(0,0,0,0.32); so it sits above the measure rather than in it. Below 700px take the editor out of the item: render it as position: fixed; left: 12px; right: 12px; bottom: 12px; with the row it belongs to scrolled into view above it, and reserve its measured height as bottom padding on .b-measure so it can never cover the last row. Add to interaction-check.mjs: the computed background-color of .b-edit has alpha 1, and no .b-title outside the edited item intersects the .b-edit rectangle at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440.

biggestWin: The horizon. Seventy-nine set at 148px, then Saturday 3 October 2026, then 'Wedding day at The Orchard' — three facts in the right order, no ornament, one indigo rule beneath them — is the first thing in this suite a stranger would believe came from a studio and would pay for. It survives the flip to paper with nothing hand-tuned, and the A4 keepsake at print is the best single artifact in the lab: a stranger would put it on a fridge. The proportional measure earns its place beside it, because the sixteen empty days above the first tick are felt rather than read. What is missing is not taste in the drawing. It is that nothing yet moves, nothing yet reverses, the numbers stop agreeing the moment you touch them, and the day itself has not been designed.
